Fulfill
ful-FIL
v.
Old English fullfyllan, “to fill up, complete,” from full + fyllan (to fill). Renders the Greek plēroō, “to fill up, complete, accomplish,” teleō, “to bring to an end,” and the Hebrew mālē’, “to fill, to fulfill.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To fulfill is to bring to fullness or completion—to fill up what was begun, to accomplish what was promised, to complete what was prefigured. Two biblical uses dominate. First and supremely, Christ fulfills the law and the prophets: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil; all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me; that the scripture might be fulfilled is the constant refrain of the Gospels, especially Matthew and John. The Christological fulfillment is multi-layered: Christ keeps the moral law in His active obedience; He pays the law’s penalty in His passive obedience; He embodies the law’s typological prefigurations (the Passover Lamb, the True Israel, the Greater David, the Better Adam); He fulfills the prophets’ predictions in His person, work, and kingdom. The Old Testament is, in a profound sense, an unfulfilled text whose meaning becomes plain in the Christ who fulfills it. Second, the saint fulfills the law of Christ in his life: love is the fulfilling of the law; bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ; the believer fulfills the righteousness of the law not by works to earn standing but as the Spirit-wrought fruit of life in Christ. The Father fulfills His purposes through providence (the counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations); the Spirit fulfills His ministry in applying the redemption Christ accomplished; the church fulfills the Great Commission as she carries the gospel to the nations; the saint fulfills his ministry by completing what the Lord has given him to do (I have finished my course). And the final fulfillment is eschatological: the consummation when all things in heaven and earth shall be gathered together in one in Christ, the bringing of God’s purposes to their appointed end at the day of the Lord. To fulfill is therefore a verb that gathers up the whole story: promise made, promise kept; type prefigured, type embodied; law given, law completed; mission entrusted, mission accomplished; kingdom inaugurated, kingdom consummated—all in the Christ who is Himself the great Yea and Amen of every promise of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FULFIL as to accomplish; to perform; as a promise, prophecy, or threat; to bring to full execution; to complete; to satisfy the requirements or expectations of.

expand to see more

FULFIL, v.t. — 1. To accomplish; to perform; as a promise, prophecy, or threat; to bring to full execution. Even so it must be that the scriptures should be fulfilled (Mark 14:49). 2. To complete; to bring to its end; as, to fulfil a course of years. 3. To accomplish what was intended; as, to fulfil one’s designs. 4. To answer in execution or event, as a prediction; as, to fulfil the prophecies. 5. To complete in obedience; as, to fulfil the law.

FULFILLING, ppr. — Accomplishing; performing; executing; answering in event.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:17-18 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Luke 24:44 — "And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me."

Romans 13:10 — "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."

Galatians 6:2 — "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Fulfillment is corrupted, on one side, by dispensational and liberal-critical traditions that dehistoricize, postpone, or deny the Christological fulfillment of the Old Testament; and on the other by the antinomian register that hears fulfilled as abolished, missing Christ’s explicit denial that He came to destroy the law.

expand to see more

Two interpretive traditions corrupt the doctrine of fulfillment by misplacing the Christological center. Strict dispensationalism, at its hardest forms, postpones much of the Old Testament’s promised fulfillment to a future earthly Jewish kingdom and reads the apostolic claim that the Scriptures are fulfilled in Christ as referring chiefly to a parenthetical ‘church age’ rather than as the substantive fulfillment of the Old Testament itself. Liberal-critical reading goes the other direction, dehistoricizing the texts so thoroughly that the very notion of fulfilled predictive prophecy collapses into a literary motif. Both miss the New Testament’s plain claim: all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. The Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ—His person, His work, His kingdom—and that fulfillment is the unifying claim of apostolic exegesis from Luke 24 to Revelation 22.

The opposite corruption is the antinomian register that hears fulfilled as abolished. Christ explicitly denied this in the very breath He used the word: think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. The law’s ceremonial prefigurations are fulfilled in Christ’s priestly work and so cease as types whose substance has come; the law’s civil arrangements were tied to Israel’s national situation and apply in their general equity; the law’s moral substance is the eternal righteousness of God, fulfilled by Christ on the believer’s behalf and fulfilled, by the Spirit, in the believer’s sanctified life—love is the fulfilling of the law. The verb fulfill therefore is not the cancellation of the Old Testament but its completion; not the displacement of the moral law but its embodiment in Christ and reproduction in His people. Both errors are corrected by the same biblical doctrine: the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ, and the moral law is fulfilled in the love that the Spirit produces in those united to Him.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek plēroō (to fill up, complete, accomplish) and teleō (to bring to an end); Hebrew mālē’ (to fill, to fulfill)—the great verb of promise kept, type embodied, law completed, and mission accomplished in the Christ who is Himself the Yea and Amen of every promise of God.

expand to see more

Greek plēroō (G4137) — to fill up, complete, accomplish, fulfill (the great Matthean fulfillment verb).

Greek teleō (G5055) — to bring to an end, complete, accomplish (‘it is finished’).

Hebrew mālē’ (H4390) — to fill, to fulfill, to accomplish.

Greek sumplēroō (G4845) — to fill up completely, fulfill (Luke 9:51, ‘when the time was come that he should be received up’).

Usage

"I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil—Christ’s own denial that fulfillment is abolition."

"The Old Testament is, in a profound sense, an unfulfilled text whose meaning becomes plain in the Christ who fulfills it."

"Love is the fulfilling of the law—the moral substance of the law is fulfilled, by the Spirit, in the believer’s sanctified life."
